summary: A 1970 note with thoughts on a proposed real-time clock at SRI. It discusses measuring delays on the network, including delays inside hosts, and the kinds of timing tests such a clock would enable, some of which would need synchronised clocks.

eli5.summary: To find out how long a message takes to travel, you need good clocks at both ends. This note thinks about how to build and use them.

subtitle: Early proposal for adding a clock to network hosts for delay measurements

tldr.problem: Early network researchers had no way to measure delays inside hosts, only the time between hosts, limiting understanding of total message delay.
tldr.mechanism: This note proposes equipping network hosts with crystal-controlled clocks providing 1 millisecond resolution and accurate synchronization.
tldr.outcome: The discussion informed future work on network timing and measurement, though practical implementation required careful hardware design.

today: This is an early proposal that helped establish the discussion about network measurement. Modern networks have standards for synchronization like NTP (RFC 958), which emerged from work like this.

sections.title: The Need for Timing
sections.content:
Early network researchers needed to understand message delays, but their measurement tools only captured the time between hosts. They could not see delays that happened inside each computer while it was processing the message. The RFC proposes adding clocks to one or more network hosts to measure these internal delays.

To truly measure end-to-end delay from one host to another would require synchronized clocks at both ends, although relative delay measurements between two clocks would not require perfect accuracy.
sections.eli5: Clocks let you measure how long something takes. If both ends have clocks, you can measure the whole journey, not just part of it.

sections.title: Clock Specifications
sections.content:
The author proposes a clock system with three key properties. First, a resolution of about 1 millisecond to capture brief delays. Second, an accuracy of about 1 part in 10,000,000 so that two clocks would stay reasonably synchronized over many hours. Third, a range of about 24 hours of continuous measurement.

The proposal notes that a crystal-controlled clock could meet these requirements at moderate cost, though hardware considerations would be important: achieving 1 millisecond resolution might require entirely hardware-based implementation rather than a location in core memory that is incremented at each clock pulse.
sections.eli5: A good clock needs to be fast enough to catch quick changes, accurate enough to stay right for hours, and remember a whole day's worth of time.

sections.title: Practical Implementation
sections.content:
The author describes existing clocks at UCLA on their Sigma 7 computer. Two clocks were available, and one had a resolution of about 2 milliseconds, which might be usable for some internal host measurements. However, it lacked the long-term accuracy needed for absolute measurements between hosts.

The challenge was not just having a clock but providing an interface that let the host read it accurately. The note closes by inviting the working group to share opinions on the design before the protocol was finalized.
sections.eli5: Building a clock is one thing; letting the computer read it fast enough is harder.
